opus-5.5.text:
Even if you had a perfect predictive model, something that could tell you exactly how any molecule would bind to a target, what its toxicity would be, how it would be metabolized, that alone doesn't solve drug design. The problem is the size of the search space. Chemical space is astronomically large. People throw around numbers like ten to the sixty possible drug-like molecules, and you can't enumerate that, let alone score every candidate, however fast your predictor is. So a perfect oracle still leaves you asking which questions to put to it.

That's where generative models come in. Instead of screening a fixed library, you learn to propose molecules that are likely to be good, and you shape the distribution you're sampling from toward the regions of chemical space that matter for your particular target and constraints. It turns an impossible search into something tractable.

And then there's the step beyond that, which is where agents come in. Real drug design isn't a single query. It's a long, iterative process with many competing objectives. You want potency, but also selectivity against related proteins, good pharmacokinetics, synthesizability, novelty for IP reasons. A medicinal chemist works through that over months, forming hypotheses, making a change, seeing what happens, backtracking. That's fundamentally a sequential decision-making problem. An agent that can reason over the problem, call predictive models as tools, generate candidates, evaluate trade-offs, and decide what to try next is much closer to how the actual work gets done.

So I think of it in layers. Predictive models are the foundation: they give you a model of the world, a kind of simulator for biology and chemistry. Generative models let you act creatively within that world. And agents let you pursue goals over long horizons using both. It's a lot like what we saw in games and other AI domains: a great value function is enormously powerful, but you still need search, a policy, and planning on top of it to really get superhuman performance. Drug design is no different.

r001.rationale: It says chemical space contains roughly 10^60 drug-like molecules and cannot be enumerated or fully scored, even with a perfect predictor, conveying that screening would cover only a negligible fraction.

r002.rationale: It describes generative models proposing molecules and steering sampling toward relevant regions of chemical space, with agents deciding what to try next.

astra-6.text:
Even if you had a perfect predictive model, you’d still have the problem of deciding what to make. A predictive model can tell you what a particular molecule will do, but the space of possible molecules is so vast that you can’t just enumerate them all and score them.

So you need something that can search that space intelligently. That’s where generative models come in: proposing molecules that satisfy the properties you care about. And in drug design, that’s a whole collection of properties. You need potency, selectivity, safety, the right exposure—and you need to be able to synthesize the molecule.

Agents take that a step further by making decisions across the discovery process. What should we generate next? Which experiment should we run? What have we learned, and how should that change our strategy? A great predictor is an incredibly valuable component, but you still need a system that turns those predictions into actions and, ultimately, a drug.

sol-6.1.text:
Even if you had a perfect predictive model, you’d still have to decide what to ask it. The space of possible molecules is enormous, so you can’t just enumerate everything, predict all their properties, and pick the best one. You need a way of searching that space, and that’s where generative models become useful: proposing molecules that are likely to satisfy the properties you care about.

And drug design isn’t really a single prediction problem. You’re balancing potency, selectivity, toxicity, whether you can actually make the molecule, and a whole range of other constraints. Then you make something, run an experiment, and use what you learn to decide what to do next. An agent can connect those steps into an iterative process.

So prediction is a crucial component, but it doesn’t by itself give you a strategy. You still need something that proposes candidates, chooses experiments, and adapts as new evidence comes in.
